outcome: No source found that settles, refutes, or otherwise moves the still-open direction of Vitushkin's conjecture (whether a purely unrectifiable compact set with non-sigma-finite H^1 measure necessarily has zero analytic capacity) since 26 January 2024; the only nearby activity is work framed by its own authors as progress adjacent to, not a resolution of, that direction.
summary: Vitushkin's conjecture (a compact K subset of C with finite H^1 measure is removable for bounded analytic functions iff it meets every rectifiable curve in a set of zero length) was already settled in the H^1-sigma-finite case before the frozen revision's date: Guy David proved it in 1998 for the finite-H^1-measure case, and combined with Tolsa's 2002-03 semiadditivity result this gives the full sigma-finite case. Mattila (1986) and later Jones-Murai showed one direction fails outright in the non-sigma-finite case (a set with zero Favard length but positive analytic capacity). The remaining open question, per the Wikipedia article and the literature, is whether the other implication holds in the non-sigma-finite setting: does purely unrectifiable / zero-Favard-length imply zero analytic capacity there? I searched extensively for any 2024-2026 work bearing on this open direction. The one paper the triage flagged, Dabrowski-Villa 'Analytic capacity and dimension of sets with plenty of big projections' (arXiv:2204.05804), was in fact first posted in April 2022 -- its only 2024 event is a June 2024 revision (v2), and its 2025 appearance is the Trans. AMS journal publication, which under Sec. 6.3 does not count as the dating event since the first written argument predates the window. Substantively, the paper proves a lower bound on analytic capacity for sets with 'plenty of big projections' (PBP), a different (sufficient-condition) class of sets, and is described by the authors themselves only as marking 'progress on an old conjecture of Vitushkin,' not as resolving the open implication. A second, genuinely 2024-dated paper, Dabrowski's solo 'Favard length and quantitative rectifiability' (arXiv:2408.03919, submitted 7 August 2024), proves a quantitative Besicovitch projection theorem (Ahlfors-regular sets with large Favard length contain big pieces of Lipschitz graphs) and again is framed by the author only as 'progress on Vitushkin's conjecture,' addressing quantitative/Favard-length questions rather than settling the stated non-sigma-finite implication. I found no paper, announcement, or digestion claiming the open direction itself was proved, disproved, or otherwise directly moved since 26 January 2024. I also searched for any AI/LLM connection to this problem or to the surrounding literature (analytic capacity, geometric measure theory, Favard length) and found none -- the AI-theorem-proving hits that surfaced (AlphaGeometry, LLM provers/verifiers) are unrelated fields with no crossover to this problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the Dabrowski-Villa PBP result and the 2024 Favard-length paper are close enough to the conjecture's spirit (both explicitly invoke Vitushkin and Favard length) that they deserve a 'progress' status rather than 'open.' I did not adopt this reading because both results concern a different, restricted class of sets (PBP sets, or Ahlfors-regular sets) rather than settling any additional case of the stated open implication (purely unrectifiable / non-sigma-finite implies zero capacity) -- per Sec 3.1 this makes them related-problem results, not case results, and the authors' own framing ('progress on', not 'resolves a case of') supports treating them as adjacent rather than as narrowing the stated question.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement proving (or disproving) that every purely unrectifiable compact set with non-sigma-finite H^1 measure has zero analytic capacity, or explicitly resolving that implication for some non-trivial subclass in a way that reduces the stated open territory -- as opposed to establishing sufficient conditions (PBP, Ahlfors-regularity, large Favard length) for positive capacity on sets outside the conjecture's hypothesis.
